annotations.annotation_text: Page 427 opens Book 3, Chapter 1 ("Shaun the Post (First Watch)") during the Age of Men phase. This passage continues Shaun floating down the Liffey in a barrel, delivering his sermon, the well-fed postman who delivers messages he cannot understand, featuring Shaun, Issy, the Rainbow Girls. The nocturnal dream-narrative layers Dublin topography, world mythology, and linguistic alchemy into polysemic prose.

JJDA: Finnegans Wake Genetic Edition. https://jjda.ie

annotations.annotation_text: The nocturnal river voyage (427.05): Shaun bobbing backwards inside his barrel down the River Liffey through nocturnal Dublin, swept by the tide toward Dublin Bay.
sources: Bishop, John. Joyce's Book of the Dark. https://archive.org/details/joycesbookofdark0000bish

annotations.annotation_text: Fraternal archetype "Shaun" on page 427 ("Shaun the Post (First Watch)"): the opposing sons — Shem the Penman (introvert artist, tree, darkness) and Shaun the Post (extrovert politician, stone, light) — manifest here within Shaun floating down the Liffey in a barrel, delivering his sermon, the well-fed postman who delivers messages he cannot understand. Their Brunonian dialectic of coinciding opposites propels the chapter's conflict during this Age of Men phase.
sources: Atherton, James S. The Books at the Wake. https://archive.org/details/booksatwake0000athe
Norris, Margot. The Decentered Universe of Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/decentereduniver0000norr
Gordon, John. Finnegans Wake: A Plot Summary. https://johngordonfinnegan.weebly.com

annotations.annotation_text: Classical parody (427.15): invokes Diogenes the Cynic philosopher who lived in a ceramic storage jar ('tub') in Athens, ironically juxtaposing ancient ascetic wisdom with Shaun's gluttonous bourgeois materialism.
sources: Contemporary Literature Press: Classical Lexicon. https://editura.mttlc.ro

annotations.annotation_text: Mid-page polysemic node on page 427 ("Shaun the Post (First Watch)"): Joyce weaves multilingual puns across 60+ languages — etymological roots from the Contemporary Literature Press lexicons (Romanian, Scandinavian, Slavic, Classical) intersect with local Dublin speech rhythms. The Age of Men dream-logic transforms ordinary syntax into a palimpsest of global literary and mythic references.
sources: Tindall, William York. A Reader's Guide to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/readersguidetofi00tind
Contemporary Literature Press: Multilingual Lexicons for FW. https://editura.mttlc.ro
Atherton, James S. The Books at the Wake. https://archive.org/details/booksatwake0000athe

annotations.annotation_text: Egyptian myth of Osiris (427.25): Osiris sealed inside a floating cedar chest by Set and cast into the Nile, drifting across the sea to Byblos before being resurrected by Isis.
sources: Troy, Mark L. Mummeries of Resurrection. http://www.rosenlake.net
